outcome: Design an awareness, education, or training intervention and identify evidence that it improved the intended behavior rather than only completion counts.

sections.body: Awareness builds broad recognition of security expectations and reporting paths. Education builds understanding of concepts and why decisions matter. Training develops a role-specific skill through instruction and practice. Use risk and audience to decide what is needed: an engineer may need secure-development practice, a finance team may need payment-verification drills, and all staff may need a current reporting path for suspicious messages.
keyPoints: Different roles need different depth and practice.
A security champion can extend local feedback but does not replace accountable program ownership.
sections.title: Match learning to the decision people must make

sections.body: Define an intended behavior and evidence before launching a campaign. Useful measures can include reporting quality and time, adoption of a secure process, error reduction, role-skill demonstration, and recurring-risk trends; completion and click rates need context and should not become punitive scoreboards. Review content when threats, technology, policy, or business practices change, including emerging technology and social-engineering patterns.
keyPoints: Measure behavior and process improvement, not only attendance.
Refresh content from risk signals, incidents, and material change.
sections.title: Measure outcomes and keep content current

sections.body: Select awareness, education, or role-specific training based on the behavior and decision needed. Use methods such as social-engineering and phishing exercises, security champions, gamification, targeted practice, and clear reporting paths without treating failure as a punishment metric. Review content periodically for emerging technology and trend changes such as cryptocurrency, AI, and blockchain, and for changed local risks. Evaluate effectiveness through defined behavior, reporting quality and time, error reduction, participation, scenario performance, and business context; completion alone is not proof. Failure modes include generic annual content, deceptive metrics, ignored feedback, and training that does not match the learner's authority or task.
keyPoints: Name the accountable owner, decision criterion, and evidence for each applicable outline topic.
Record the failure consequence and escalation or review trigger rather than assuming a policy label proves operation.
